deduplicationLog.reason: Exact same finding: missing access control on dispatch(). Both identify ATokenDispatcher.sol:44. ECON-001 has far more detailed analysis including multi-dispatcher attack scenarios, so it is used as the primary description.

Same root cause: BalancerPooler 1:1 decimal-normalized minting assumes price parity. CODE-006 flags the donation imbalance. ECON-002 specifically identifies yield-bearing tokens (sUSDS) as the vector and quantifies the arbitrage leakage. Same code location.

Same root cause: missing validation that price > 0. CODE-008 notes setPrice and decay paths. ECON-004 notes registerDispatcher path and permanent stuck-at-zero due to growth formula. Combined into unified finding covering both entry points.

Closely related root cause: CODE-005 (infinite approval with no revocation) and CODE-009 (no deregistration mechanism) are two facets of the same design gap -- once a dispatcher is registered, it has permanent unlimited token access with no way to revoke. A single finding with both aspects is more actionable.
Exact same finding: emergencyWithdraw drains Accumulator tokens. Same contract:function:line. ECON-006 has the better cross-dispatcher economic analysis.

Same root cause: unchecked ERC20 transfer return values. CODE-004 identifies NFTMinter.sol:132. ECON-007 identifies NFTMinter.sol:187 and Gather.sol:67. Combined into single finding covering all unchecked locations. NOTE: CODE-004 cites NFTMinter.sol:132 (transferFrom in mint), but that call is effectively checked by the balance-before/after pattern on lines 131-133. The actually-vulnerable locations are the transfer() calls without balance checks. Severity adjusted: the mint() transferFrom is implicitly checked, reducing impact to the emergencyWithdraw and Gather.dispatch transfer calls, which are LOW severity paths.
Unique finding from code scanner. Cross-contract reentrancy in mint() -- price state updated after external dispatch call and ERC1155 callback. Not duplicated by any econ-scanner finding.
Unique finding. BalancerPooler minBptAmountOut=0 allows sandwich attacks. Not duplicated by econ scanner (ECON-002 is about the 1:1 ratio, not the slippage on BPT output).
Unique finding. BPT tokens permanently locked in BalancerPooler with no recovery mechanism. Not reported by econ scanner.

Unique finding from econ scanner. Integer rounding stagnation in price growth formula. Distinct from zero-price issue (ECON-004/CODE-008) because this affects non-zero prices where price * growthBasisPoints < 10000.
Unique finding from econ scanner. Front-running/MEV extraction on rising price curve due to missing maxPrice slippage parameter. Not reported by code scanner.
Unique finding from econ scanner. No upper bound on growthBasisPoints allows overflow/DoS. Not reported by code scanner.

deduplicatedFindings.title: Missing access control on dispatcher dispatch() allows anyone to drain tokens from NFTMinter
deduplicatedFindings.description: The dispatch() function on ATokenDispatcher (and all concrete dispatchers: Burner, Gather, BalancerPooler, Accumulator) is external with only a whenNotPaused modifier -- no caller restriction. The first parameter 'minter' is caller-supplied and used as the address to pull tokens from via transferFrom(). During registerDispatcher(), NFTMinter grants type(uint256).max approval to each dispatcher. Any external caller can invoke dispatch(nftMinterAddress, amount) on any registered dispatcher to force-pull the NFTMinter's entire token balance. This is especially devastating when an Accumulator dispatcher is used alongside a Burner or Gather dispatcher for the same prime token: tokens meant to accumulate can be force-burned (Burner), force-redirected (Gather), or force-donated to Balancer at bad timing (BalancerPooler).
deduplicatedFindings.impact: Complete loss of all ERC20 token balances held by the NFTMinter contract. Tokens accumulated via the Accumulator dispatcher can be irreversibly burned (Burner), redirected to Gather recipient (potential profit for attacker), or force-donated to Balancer pool. Even with a single dispatcher type, an attacker can front-run legitimate protocol operations.
deduplicatedFindings.recommendation: Add access control to dispatch(). The simplest fix is require(msg.sender == _minter) in ATokenDispatcher.dispatch() or each concrete override.

deduplicatedFindings.title: Cross-contract reentrancy in NFTMinter.mint() -- price state updated after external calls and ERC1155 callback
deduplicatedFindings.description: In NFTMinter.mint(), the execution order is: (1) read price from storage (line 128), (2) transferFrom user (line 132), (3) call dispatcher.dispatch() which makes external calls (line 136), (4) update config.price in storage (line 139), (5) _mint ERC1155 which triggers onERC1155Received callback to recipient (line 142). The price state update at step 4 occurs after the external dispatch call at step 3. If the dispatcher makes a callback (e.g., BalancerPooler's vault.unlock triggers unlockCallback) or if the recipient's onERC1155Received callback re-enters mint(), the attacker can mint multiple NFTs at the same price before the growth increment is applied. The ERC1155 _mint at step 5 also triggers a callback to the recipient before the function returns.
deduplicatedFindings.impact: An attacker can mint multiple NFTs at the same price by re-entering via the ERC1155 callback, bypassing the intended price growth mechanism. Each re-entrant mint uses the stale price, effectively getting a discount proportional to the number of re-entrant calls times the growth rate.
deduplicatedFindings.root_cause_snippet:
// NFTMinter.sol:128-142 -- state update after external calls
uint256 price = config.price;                                    // step 1: read
ATokenDispatcher(config.dispatcher).dispatch(address(this), actualReceived); // step 3: external call
config.price = price + (price * config.growthBasisPoints) / 10000;          // step 4: state update
_mint(recipient, CLAIM_TOKEN_ID, 1, "");                                   // step 5: ERC1155 callback
deduplicatedFindings.recommendation: Apply checks-effects-interactions: update config.price before the dispatch() call and the _mint() call. Alternatively, add a reentrancy guard (ReentrancyGuard from OpenZeppelin).

deduplicatedFindings.title: BalancerPooler 1:1 decimal-normalized minting of phUSD assumes price parity with yield-bearing prime tokens
deduplicatedFindings.description: BalancerPooler._normalizeToPhUSD() only performs decimal conversion, minting phUSD at a strict 1:1 ratio (decimal-adjusted) with the incoming prime token. The Accumulator's NatSpec specifically mentions 'tokens like sUSDS' as a prime token. sUSDS is a yield-bearing stablecoin whose value appreciates over time relative to 1 USD. If sUSDS is the prime token, the BalancerPooler donates 1 sUSDS (worth >1 USD) + 1 phUSD (worth 1 USD) to the pool. This imbalance is systematically extracted by arbitrageurs after every donation. For sUSDS at a 5% premium, approximately 2.5% of each donation's value is extractable.
deduplicatedFindings.impact: Systematic value leakage from every donation to the Balancer pool. Arbitrageurs extract the price imbalance between the yield-bearing prime token and phUSD. The leakage grows over time as the yield-bearing token appreciates. This affects existing Balancer pool LPs and means the protocol donates more value than intended.
deduplicatedFindings.recommendation: Use an oracle or the prime token's exchange rate function (e.g., sUSDS.convertToAssets()) to determine the correct phUSD mint amount. Alternatively, document this as intentional design if phUSD is meant to track the prime token's value rather than USD.

deduplicatedFindings.title: Unchecked ERC20 transfer/transferFrom return values across multiple contracts
deduplicatedFindings.description: Multiple contracts use IERC20.transfer() and IERC20.transferFrom() without checking return values. Some ERC20 tokens (notably USDT) return false instead of reverting on failure. The affected locations are: NFTMinter.emergencyWithdraw() line 187 (transfer), Gather.dispatch() line 67 (transfer to recipient), BalancerPooler.unlockCallback() lines 81 and 87 (transfers to vault). Note: The transferFrom calls in NFTMinter.mint() (line 132) and the dispatcher dispatch() functions are effectively guarded by the balance-before/after pattern, which provides implicit verification. The unguarded transfer() calls are the actual risk.
deduplicatedFindings.impact: For tokens that return false on failure, transfers could silently fail. In emergencyWithdraw, the owner would believe tokens were rescued when they were not. In Gather.dispatch, tokens would accumulate in the Gather contract with no recovery mechanism. In BalancerPooler, tokens could fail to reach the vault causing accounting discrepancies.
deduplicatedFindings.recommendation: Use SafeERC20.safeTransfer() and SafeERC20.safeTransferFrom() from OpenZeppelin for all ERC20 transfer calls.

deduplicatedFindings.title: Irrevocable infinite token approval to dispatchers with no deregistration mechanism
deduplicatedFindings.description: registerDispatcher() grants type(uint256).max approval to the dispatcher for its prime token (line 106), but there is no mechanism to revoke this approval or deregister a dispatcher. Once registered, a dispatcher permanently retains unlimited access to pull the prime token from NFTMinter. The dispatcherToIndex mapping prevents re-registration but there is no way to remove an entry, revoke the approval, or replace a compromised dispatcher. Combined with DEDUP-001 (missing access control on dispatch()), this means a registered dispatcher is a permanent, irrevocable drain vector. Even if DEDUP-001 is fixed with an onlyMinter check, a compromised or buggy dispatcher contract retains infinite approval forever.
deduplicatedFindings.impact: Permanently registered dispatchers retain unlimited token access. If a dispatcher contract is compromised, upgraded maliciously (if upgradeable), or has a bug discovered post-registration, there is no way to revoke its access to NFTMinter's tokens. The only mitigation is pausing the dispatcher, but pause does not revoke the underlying ERC20 approval.
deduplicatedFindings.recommendation: Add a deregisterDispatcher() function that revokes the ERC20 approval (approve to 0) and removes the dispatcher from mappings. Alternatively, approve only the needed amount per dispatch rather than infinite approval.

deduplicatedFindings.title: Price can be set to zero via setPrice or registerDispatcher, enabling permanent free minting
deduplicatedFindings.description: Neither registerDispatcher() nor setPrice() validate that the price is non-zero. If initialPrice is 0 or the owner calls setPrice(index, 0), users can mint NFTs for free. The growth formula config.price = 0 + (0 * growthBasisPoints) / 10000 = 0 means the price can never recover from zero regardless of growthBasisPoints -- it is permanently stuck. Additionally, setPrice allows the owner to reset a healthy price to zero at any time. While this requires owner action, a misconfiguration or compromised owner creates a permanent free-minting condition. The transferFrom with amount=0 succeeds on most ERC20 tokens, so the mint completes without transferring any tokens.
deduplicatedFindings.impact: Unlimited free minting of claim NFTs. If NFTs carry economic rights (yield claims, governance weight), this enables unbounded value extraction. Price is permanently stuck at zero with no recovery path except another setPrice call.
deduplicatedFindings.recommendation: Add require(initialPrice > 0) in registerDispatcher() and require(newPrice > 0) in setPrice(). Consider a minimum price floor.

deduplicatedFindings.title: emergencyWithdraw can drain tokens intentionally accumulated by Accumulator dispatcher
deduplicatedFindings.description: emergencyWithdraw() allows the owner to withdraw the entire balance of any ERC20 from NFTMinter. The Accumulator dispatcher is a no-op that intentionally leaves tokens in NFTMinter for later consumption by BalancerPooler. emergencyWithdraw does not distinguish between 'stuck' tokens and tokens intentionally accumulated. The owner can accidentally or intentionally drain accumulated tokens, breaking the intended accumulate-then-pool economic flow. While this is owner-only, it represents a centralization risk with no accounting safeguard.
deduplicatedFindings.impact: Owner can drain tokens accumulated for BalancerPooler consumption, breaking the intended token flow. All accumulated tokens intended for Balancer pool donations are lost. This is a centralization/admin trust issue rather than an external attack vector.
deduplicatedFindings.recommendation: Track accumulated balances per-dispatcher and ensure emergencyWithdraw only rescues genuinely stuck tokens (excess beyond tracked accumulations). Alternatively, document clearly as intended admin capability.

deduplicatedFindings.title: Price growth stagnation due to integer rounding -- small prices permanently stop growing
deduplicatedFindings.description: The price growth formula config.price = price + (price * growthBasisPoints) / 10000 rounds to zero when price * growthBasisPoints < 10000. For example: price = 99 wei with growthBasisPoints = 100 (1%) yields increment = 99 * 100 / 10000 = 0. Once stagnated, the price never increases regardless of further mints, enabling unlimited minting at the stagnated (potentially negligible) cost. This is distinct from the zero-price issue (DEDUP-006) because it affects non-zero prices that are simply too small relative to the growth rate.
deduplicatedFindings.impact: If the price stagnates at a low value, users can mint unlimited claim NFTs at negligible cost. If NFTs carry economic rights, this allows unbounded extraction. Even without direct economic rights, unlimited NFT supply inflation dilutes existing holders.
deduplicatedFindings.recommendation: Add a minimum price threshold. Alternatively, use a fixed additive increment in addition to the multiplicative growth, or require that price * growthBasisPoints >= 10000 at registration.

deduplicatedFindings.title: BalancerPooler.addLiquidity uses minBptAmountOut=0 allowing sandwich attacks on liquidity provision
deduplicatedFindings.description: In BalancerPooler.unlockCallback(), the AddLiquidityParams are constructed with minBptAmountOut: 0. This means the contract accepts any amount of BPT tokens in return for its liquidity donation, including zero. A sandwich attacker can manipulate the pool's reserves before the addLiquidity call to extract maximum value. The attacker front-runs by skewing pool ratios, the BalancerPooler donates at the manipulated ratio accepting any BPT output, then the attacker back-runs to restore pool balance and profit from the manipulation. Note: the AddLiquidityKind is DONATION, which may mitigate this depending on Balancer V3's DONATION semantics (donations may not mint BPT). This should be verified against the Balancer V3 specification.
deduplicatedFindings.impact: If DONATION kind mints BPT proportional to the donation (or if the kind is changed in the future), sandwich attackers can extract value from every liquidity addition. Even with DONATION semantics, the permanently zero slippage tolerance is a code-level deficiency that should be addressed.
deduplicatedFindings.recommendation: If DONATION kind does not mint BPT in Balancer V3, document this assumption explicitly. If it does mint BPT, calculate a minimum acceptable BPT output based on current pool state and apply a slippage tolerance. Consider adding an oracle-based sanity check for pool ratios before donating.

deduplicatedFindings.title: BPT tokens received from addLiquidity are permanently locked in BalancerPooler contract
deduplicatedFindings.description: If the addLiquidity DONATION call returns BPT tokens to the BalancerPooler contract (address(this) is the 'to' parameter), those tokens are permanently locked -- there is no function to withdraw or use them. The contract has no sweep/withdraw mechanism for any tokens. Note: if Balancer V3 DONATION kind does not mint BPT, this issue is moot. But the 'to: address(this)' parameter suggests the code expects to receive BPT.
deduplicatedFindings.impact: BPT tokens (representing LP positions in the Balancer pool) accumulate in the BalancerPooler contract with no recovery mechanism. These tokens may have economic value (LP fees, governance rights) that is permanently lost.
deduplicatedFindings.recommendation: Add a function to withdraw or forward BPT tokens to a designated recipient (e.g., the owner or a treasury). Alternatively, set the 'to' parameter to the intended BPT recipient directly.

deduplicatedFindings.title: Front-running mint transactions exploits rising price curve -- no maxPrice slippage protection
deduplicatedFindings.description: The mint price increases after each mint via the growth formula. Since the price is determined by on-chain state at execution time and there is no maxPrice parameter, users have no slippage protection. An MEV searcher can front-run a pending mint, causing the victim to pay a higher price than expected. With all NFTs being the same ERC1155 token ID (CLAIM_TOKEN_ID = 1), the front-runner's NFT has identical economic rights but was acquired at a lower cost. The extracted value per front-run equals price * growthBasisPoints / 10000.
deduplicatedFindings.impact: Users consistently overpay for NFT mints. At 2% growth (200 bps) and 100 USDC price, each front-run extracts 2 USDC. This represents systematic MEV extraction from all legitimate minters.
deduplicatedFindings.recommendation: Add a maxPrice parameter to mint(): require(config.price <= maxPrice, 'Price exceeds max'). This provides slippage protection against front-running.

deduplicatedFindings.title: No upper bound on growthBasisPoints allows price overflow and dispatcher bricking
deduplicatedFindings.description: No maximum cap on growthBasisPoints in registerDispatcher() or setGrowthFactor(). Extreme values (e.g., 1,000,000 = 10,000%) cause exponential price growth that overflows uint256 after a few mints (starting at 1e18, overflow after ~18 mints at 10,000% growth). The overflow reverts all subsequent mint transactions, permanently bricking the dispatcher. This is an owner-only parameter but lacks any validation to prevent accidental misconfiguration.
deduplicatedFindings.impact: Permanent DoS for a dispatcher if price overflows. Even without overflow, excessively high growth rates make NFTs economically inaccessible after a few mints.
deduplicatedFindings.recommendation: Add a maximum cap on growthBasisPoints (e.g., 10000 = 100% per mint). Add overflow protection in the growth formula.
